scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

prediction.raw: **YTA (Yes, You're the Asshole)** **Here's why:** ### 1️️ **You deliberately weaponized your mother's pain** - You *knew* your parents' divorce deeply upset her (she explicitly said "I tried my best" and "how the divorce upset her"). - Telling her **"you're the reason I won't wear white"** directly tied her personal trauma to your aesthetic choice. That’s not just "honesty"— it’s using her vulnerability as ammunition. - *Example:* If someone said, "I won’t adopt a dog because your ex was a terrible pet owner," you’d recognize it as cruel. This is the same dynamic. ### 2️️ **"I shouldn’t have to justify myself" is valid... but only if you *didn’t* force a painful confession** - You *did* justify yourself multiple times (Queen Victoria, "not innocent," "colored dresses look nicer"). - **The problem wasn’t that you had to justify it**— it’s that you *chose* to escalate to the most hurtful explanation when she asked "why." - When someone asks "why," they’re seeking understanding, not a psychological landmine. You could’ve said: > * "I associate white with the divorce, so I’d rather choose a color that feels hopeful for me." > * "I’m not comfortable with white because of our family history, but I’d love to talk about colors that *do* feel right for me." **Instead, you said:** " *You’re the reason* I won’t wear white." That’s not "honesty"— it’s a calculated emotional strike. ### 3️️ **"Only my fiancé’s opinion matters" is dismissive and immature** - Your mother isn’t just "a random person"— she’s invested in your wedding. - Telling her * " only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiancé"* after she’s emotionally vulnerable is a power move. It’s not "asserting boundaries"— it’s gaslighting her right to care. - **Boundaries are healthy** (e.g., "I’ve made my decision, and I’d appreciate your support"), but **" your opinion doesn’t matter" is a knife twist.** ### 4️️ **You’re conflating "valid feelings" with "appropriate behavior"** - Your * feelings* about white dresses are 100% valid (divorce trauma is real). - But **"valid feelings don’t excuse cruel delivery."** - If you’d said: * "I’ve always struggled with white because of our family history, and I’d rather choose a color that feels healing for me"*— she’d likely have been hurt but * understood*. - Instead, you said: * "You broke the tradition, so I won’t wear white"*— which frames her as the * cause* of your choice. That’s not just insensitive; it’s actively harmful. ### ✨ **What to do now:** - **Apologize specifically:** * "I’m so sorry I said ‘ you’re the reason’— that was cruel and unfair. I didn’t mean to hurt you. I associate white with the divorce, but that’s my own baggage, not your fault."* - **Reframe the conversation:** * "I’d love to find a color that feels meaningful for * both* of us. Can we look at options together?"* - **Remember:** You get to choose your dress, but you don’t get to * weaponize your mother’s pain to get it*. **Bottom line:** Your feelings are valid, but your words were a deliberate emotional attack. YTA. *(P.S. If you’re truly committed to not wearing white, that’s your right—but do it with grace. Your mother’s tears are a sign you crossed a line.)*
